project.name: NutriKitchen
project.summary: A personal, AI-enabled nutrition, meal-planning, and kitchen-inventory application that connects food consumption, nutritional goals, available ingredients, and grocery activity.
project.vision: Help a user understand what they eat, choose a suitable next meal, and manage ingredients at home, while clearly communicating estimates and uncertainty.
project.audience: Initially a single user's personal project and learning vehicle; future multi-user product scope is not yet defined.

sourceAndScope.representation: Structured summary and project handoff derived from the conversation; not a verbatim transcript.
sourceAndScope.scopeNote: This brief consolidates the product idea, learning goals, engineering expectations, proposed roadmap, and next step. Decisions marked proposed remain open for requirements discovery.

userLearningProfile.experience: Approximately 3 years of QA experience and 1 year in development at the time of the conversation.
userLearningProfile.knownFoundation: Java and Spring Boot experience was mentioned; depth in individual topics should be checked as needed.
learningGoals: Build backend engineering depth through a real project
Learn new technologies incrementally and in context
Understand why engineering practices and tools are used
mentoringApproach: Explain unfamiliar concepts when they become relevant
Connect concepts to the project and discuss trade-offs
Let the learner implement and reason through solutions
Review and debug collaboratively instead of always replacing work with finished code
Avoid reteaching fundamentals already understood; check understanding as work proceeds

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Nutrition tracking
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Record meals and estimate calories, protein, carbohydrates, fats, and other nutrients against user-defined goals.

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Meal management
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Record home-cooked meals, snacks, and restaurant orders; distinguish ordered food from food confirmed as consumed.

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Pantry and ingredient inventory
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Track purchased, confirmed, estimated, and remaining quantities; account for units, recipe use, corrections, low-stock thresholds, and expiry where available.

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Next-meal recommendations
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Recommend suitable meals using remaining nutrition goals, dietary restrictions, preferences, preparation time, and pantry availability; explain recommendation reasons.

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Grocery order and receipt import
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Reduce manual entry by importing grocery details through authorized integrations where available, with invoice/receipt import and manual correction as practical initial paths.

productVisionAndCapabilities.name: Alerts and automation
productVisionAndCapabilities.description: Generate low-stock or expiry warnings and, later, shopping lists and personalized suggestions.

exampleEndToEndFlow: A grocery purchase is imported or confirmed and creates pantry stock.
The user logs a home-cooked meal or restaurant meal.
Nutrition is calculated or estimated and added to the user's daily totals.
For recipe-based cooking, ingredient consumption is applied to inventory with compatible units.
Remaining nutrition goals and available ingredients inform the next-meal recommendation.
Inventory thresholds or consumption trends can trigger low-stock alerts.
The user can correct inventory and meal details when the system's estimates are wrong.
keyProductConstraintsAndOpenQuestions: Do not assume Blinkit, Zepto, Instamart, Swiggy, or Zomato expose consumer order-history APIs. Investigate authorized access before committing to direct integrations.
Prefer invoice/receipt upload plus user confirmation and manual entry as an initial import route if provider access is unavailable.
An order is not proof the food was consumed; preserve distinct order and consumption records/states.
Nutrition values for restaurant meals, brands, and approximate portions may be estimates; show provenance and uncertainty rather than implying false precision.
Inventory is inherently uncertain when meals or purchases are not logged; distinguish confirmed, estimated, and unknown stock and allow correction.
Model units and raw-versus-cooked ingredient conversions explicitly; do not subtract incompatible quantities.
Personal nutrition goals and recommendation rules need requirements discovery and should not be framed as medical advice.

engineeringExpectations.developmentLifecycle: Use an iterative, practical Agile-inspired SDLC for every feature: requirement analysis, specification and acceptance criteria, design, implementation, testing, code review, CI/CD, deployment, monitoring, and maintenance.
principles: Understand the requirement, business rules, edge cases, and failure cases before implementation
Build maintainable software with clear responsibilities and separation of concerns
Apply SOLID and design patterns when they address a real design need; avoid ceremony and needless abstractions
Introduce complexity gradually and justify important technology and architecture choices
Treat tests as part of development and use the learner's QA background as a strength
Keep lightweight documentation current with the product
Make security, reliability, observability, and production readiness part of delivery
Ensure the learner understands the code and trade-offs
featureWorkflow: Create or refine an issue describing the problem
Define requirements, edge cases, and acceptance criteria
Design the relevant domain model, API, data changes, and component responsibilities
Implement on a focused Git branch with meaningful commits
Add or update appropriate automated tests
Run build, tests, and relevant quality checks
Review the diff for correctness, security, maintainability, performance, and unnecessary complexity
Update README, API docs, diagrams, ADRs, or runbooks as appropriate
Deploy, observe, maintain, and learn from results as relevant to project maturity

testingStrategy.purpose: Fast checks of focused business logic, such as nutrition calculations and recommendation scoring.
Verify persistence and components together, including PostgreSQL behavior.
Verify HTTP contracts, validation, authorization, and error responses.
Check compatibility with external provider boundaries when integrations exist.
Verify a small number of complete user workflows.
Assess important latency/load behavior and protection of user data as product risk grows.

engineeringExpectations.codeReviewDistinction: Separate genuine defects from maintainability concerns and stylistic preferences.

documentationArtifacts.purpose: Functional and non-functional requirements and acceptance criteria
Architecture Decision Records documenting context, alternatives, decision, and consequences

engineeringExpectations.ciCd: Use GitHub Actions incrementally for compile/build, unit and integration tests, static analysis, and artifact creation; introduce automated deployment later.
productionEngineeringTopics: Secrets management and secure input handling
Logging, metrics, tracing, and health checks
Timeouts, retries, idempotency, graceful failure, and rate limiting

proposedArchitectureAndStack.architecture: Start as a modular monolith with clear domain/module boundaries. Evolve only when requirements or operational evidence justify it.

backend.language: Java 21 or a currently supported LTS version; confirm at project setup
tests: Testcontainers when integration testing against PostgreSQL

supportingTopics: TanStack Query or a comparable data-fetching library
Charting library if nutrition summaries need charts
frontend.alternative: Flutter if mobile-first native applications become the priority; avoid learning React, TypeScript, Flutter, and Java simultaneously at the outset.

integrations.initialApproach: Normalize provider data into internal models. Start with reliable manual entry or receipt/invoice import where official consumer APIs are unavailable.
laterOptions: Email receipt parsing only after privacy, access, and feasibility review
Resilient HTTP clients such as Spring WebClient and Resilience4j when needed

conditionalTechnologies.introduceWhen: Reproducible local environments or deployment packaging are needed.
A concrete caching, rate limiting, or coordination need appears.
There are justified asynchronous event-processing needs and simpler mechanisms are insufficient.
Deployment scale/operations justify orchestration; not an initial requirement.
Natural-language meal entry, receipt interpretation, or explanations add value after deterministic validation paths exist.
The app needs grounded answers over a maintained knowledge collection; not merely for ordinary database lookup.
Operational observability needs grow beyond logs and health checks.

architectureNotes: Keep business logic independent from provider-specific response formats behind appropriate boundaries.
Validate AI-produced structures and use deterministic backend logic for nutrition calculations and persistence.
Enforce authorization and permissions server-side; never give an LLM unrestricted database access.
Use transactions and concurrency controls for meal logging and inventory changes where atomicity is required.
Use idempotency to protect against duplicate imports or repeated operations.

technologyRoadmap.name: Build the foundation
technologyRoadmap.goal: Deliver a working nutrition-tracking backend with a database.
technologyRoadmap.milestone: A user can record a meal and food items, calculate nutrition, and see daily totals.

technologyRoadmap.name: Recipes and pantry
technologyRoadmap.goal: Track recipes, ingredients, and reliable inventory changes.
technologies: Optimistic locking or other justified concurrency control
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Create recipes, log meals, update pantry quantities, and handle concurrent inventory changes reliably.

technologyRoadmap.name: Usable frontend
technologyRoadmap.goal: Use the application through a browser.
technologies: Frontend testing tools selected during implementation
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Use dashboard, meal log, recipe manager, and pantry screens against real APIs.

technologyRoadmap.name: Authentication and external integrations
technologyRoadmap.goal: Protect accounts and safely integrate external food/order data.
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Import food data and grocery information through at least one feasible mechanism; retain manual correction and distinguish orders from consumption.

technologyRoadmap.name: Recommendation engine
technologyRoadmap.goal: Recommend meals using remaining nutrition needs, preferences, and actual inventory.
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Rank and explain suitable recipes based on nutritional fit and ingredients available.

technologyRoadmap.name: AI and computer vision
technologyRoadmap.goal: Reduce tedious data entry and support natural interaction after trustworthy core logic exists.
technologyRoadmap.milestone: AI can parse descriptions or receipts into candidate structured data, with user confirmation and backend validation before saving.

technologyRoadmap.name: Asynchronous processing
technologyRoadmap.goal: Move suitable slow or event-based work out of synchronous request paths.
technologies: Redis and/or Kafka only when justified
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Process a justified background workflow reliably and observe its status.

technologyRoadmap.name: Analytics and prediction
technologyRoadmap.goal: Estimate consumption and improve useful shopping/recommendation insights.
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Provide useful, explainable consumption or low-stock estimates based on observed history.

technologyRoadmap.name: Production deployment
technologyRoadmap.goal: Deploy and operate the application with production-minded safeguards.
technologies: Cloud platform selected when requirements are known
technologyRoadmap.milestone: Deploy a documented release with automated checks, health visibility, and a basic recovery plan.

milestones: Requirements and domain model agreed before Java implementation
Nutrition tracking backend and PostgreSQL schema working
Recipe and pantry workflows with safe transactional behavior
At least one practical, authorized external data-import path
Validated AI-assisted entry only where it improves usability
Documented deployment with CI/CD and operational visibility

firstNextStep.name: Requirements engineering and domain modelling
firstNextStep.instruction: Begin Phase 1, Step 1. Define what User, FoodItem, Meal, and MealItem mean in this system; write functional and non-functional requirements, business rules, edge cases, and acceptance criteria; sketch the initial domain/database model before writing Java code.
initialQuestions: Is the first release single-user or multi-user?
Which meal-entry paths belong in the MVP?
Which nutrients and units are in MVP scope?
How are nutrition targets entered and represented?
What level of ingredient and pantry tracking is required for the first release?
How should estimates, unknown values, and user corrections be represented?
firstDeliverables: Acceptance criteria and key failure cases
ADR for initial architecture and stack choices
